description: Logical connectives, equality and comparison operators, numeric and structural predicates, Boolean-function algebra (minimization, satisfiability, truth tables) and the special constants Infinity, Indeterminate and Null.

tools.name: And
tools.description: Logical conjunction e1 && e2 && ...; evaluates arguments left to right and stops at the first False (short-circuit), so later arguments may be expensive or invalid for earlier failures. Symbolic when arguments are not True/False, and simplifiable with LogicalExpand or BooleanMinimize.
tools.example:
x > 0 && IntegerQ[x]
And @@ Map[PrimeQ, {2, 3, 5}] (* True *)
Select[data, 0 < #[[1]] < 10 && #[[2]] != 0 &]
tools.notes: And has attribute HoldAll; use AllTrue for a list of predicates. Or (||) and Not (!) are the companions; Xor, Nand, Nor, Implies and Equivalent complete the connectives.

tools.name: Or
tools.description: Logical disjunction e1 || e2 || ...; evaluates left to right and stops at the first True. Remains symbolic for non-Boolean arguments and can be used with Reduce, Solve and Simplify as a logical combination of conditions.
tools.example:
Reduce[x^2 == 1 || x == 3, x]
Or @@ Map[EvenQ, {1, 3, 4}] (* True *)

tools.name: Not
tools.description: Logical negation !e. Yields True/False for Boolean input and stays symbolic otherwise; Not[a == b] is displayed as a != b and Not[a < b] as a >= b under Simplify.
tools.example:
Select[names, !StringStartsQ[#, "_"] &]
Simplify[!(x > 3)] (* x <= 3 *)

tools.name: Xor
tools.description: Exclusive or: True when an odd number of arguments are True. Together with Nand, Nor, Xnor, Implies and Equivalent it completes the Boolean connectives used in circuit design and BooleanConvert forms.
tools.example:
Xor[True, True, False] (* False *)
BooleanTable[Xor[a, b], {a, b}]
BooleanConvert[Xor[a, b], "DNF"]

tools.name: Implies
tools.description: Logical implication p => q (False only when p is True and q is False); Equivalent[p, q, ...] tests logical equivalence. Both are used in Boolean algebra, Reduce conditions and formal proof construction (FindEquationalProof).
tools.usage:
Implies[p, q]
p \[Implies] q
Equivalent[p, q, ...]
tools.example:
BooleanConvert[Implies[a, b]] (* !a || b *)
TautologyQ[Equivalent[Implies[a, b], Or[Not[a], b]]] (* True *)

tools.name: Equal
tools.description: Mathematical equality lhs == rhs. Returns True/False when both sides are numbers or explicitly identical/different; otherwise stays as a symbolic equation, which is what Solve, Reduce, DSolve and NDSolve expect. Unequal (!=) is its negation. Numerical comparisons use tolerance based on the precision of the inputs.
tools.usage:
lhs == rhs
Equal[e1, e2, ...]
lhs != rhs
tools.example:
Solve[x^2 == 4, x]
1.0 == 1 (* True *)
x == x (* True *)
x == y (* stays symbolic *)
tools.notes: Use SameQ (===) for structural identity that always returns True or False; Equal on lists compares element-wise only when the structure matches.

tools.name: SameQ
tools.description: Structural identity test lhs === rhs: True only if the expressions are identical after evaluation (with numbers compared by value and precision), otherwise False - it never stays symbolic. UnsameQ (=!=) is the negation. Use it in conditionals and pattern tests where a definite Boolean is required.
tools.usage:
lhs === rhs
SameQ[e1, e2, ...]
lhs =!= rhs
tools.example:
x === y (* False *)
If[result === $Failed, Abort[]]
1 === 1.0 (* False: Integer vs Real *)

tools.name: TrueQ
tools.description: Yields True if expr is explicitly True and False otherwise, converting an undecided symbolic condition into a definite Boolean. Use it in If/While tests that might receive symbolic input.

parameters.name: expr
parameters.description: Expression, typically a condition that may not evaluate to True/False.

tools.example:
TrueQ[x > 0] (* False, since x is symbolic *)
If[TrueQ[Simplify[a^2 >= 0, a \[Element] Reals]], "proved", "unknown"]

tools.name: Less
tools.description: Ordering comparisons x < y, x <= y, x > y, x >= y (Less, LessEqual, Greater, GreaterEqual), chainable as a < b < c. They return True/False for real numbers and stay symbolic otherwise, forming the inequalities used by Reduce, Minimize, RegionPlot and ImplicitRegion.
tools.usage:
x < y
Less[x1, x2, ...]
x <= y
x > y
x >= y
x1 < x2 < x3
tools.example:
Reduce[x^2 < 4 && x > 0, x]
0 < t <= 1
Select[data, 5 < # < 10 &]
tools.notes: Complex numbers cannot be ordered; comparing them leaves the expression unevaluated. Order is the canonical-order function for arbitrary expressions.

tools.name: Between
tools.description: Tests whether x lies in the interval {min, max} (inclusive) or in any of several intervals; has an operator form Between[{min, max}][x] convenient for Select and Query. Works on numbers, dates and quantities.
tools.usage:
Between[x, {min, max}]
Between[x, {{min1, max1}, {min2, max2}, ...}]
Between[{min, max}][x]
tools.example:
Select[Range[20], Between[{5, 8}]] (* {5, 6, 7, 8} *)
Between[Today, {DateObject[{2024, 1, 1}], DateObject[{2024, 12, 31}]}]

tools.name: Positive
tools.description: Numeric sign predicates: Positive, Negative, NonPositive, NonNegative test the sign of real numbers and return False for non-real or symbolic input (unless assumptions decide it). Convenient as Select/Count criteria and as pattern tests like x_?Positive.
tools.example:
Select[{-2, 0, 3}, Positive] (* {3} *)
f[x_?NonNegative] := Sqrt[x]
Count[residuals, _?Negative]

tools.name: EvenQ
tools.description: EvenQ and OddQ test integer parity; IntegerQ tests for explicit integers (a symbol is never an integer, use Element[x, Integers] for assumptions). Together with PrimeQ and NumberQ they are the everyday numeric pattern tests.
tools.example:
Select[Range[10], EvenQ]
Cases[list, _Integer?OddQ]
IntegerQ[2.0] (* False *)
tools.notes: NumberQ is True only for explicit numeric heads; NumericQ also accepts constants like Pi and numeric functions of numbers.

tools.name: Piecewise
tools.description: Represents a piecewise function {{val1, cond1}, {val2, cond2}, ...} with an optional default (0). Piecewise expressions are first-class mathematical objects: Integrate, D, Simplify, Plot, DSolve and Minimize understand them, unlike If, which is procedural.
tools.usage:
Piecewise[{{val1, cond1}, {val2, cond2}, ...}]
Piecewise[{{val1, cond1}, ...}, default]

parameters.name: {val, cond}
parameters.description: Value and its condition, tested in order.

tools.example:
f[x_] := Piecewise[{{x^2, x < 0}, {Sin[x], 0 <= x < Pi}}, 1]
Integrate[f[x], {x, -1, 4}]
PiecewiseExpand[Abs[x] + UnitStep[x]]
tools.notes: PiecewiseExpand converts Abs, Max, UnitStep, Clip etc. into Piecewise form. Which is the procedural counterpart.

tools.name: ConditionalExpression
tools.description: Represents a value that is valid only when a condition holds; Integrate, Solve, Reduce and Simplify return it when a result depends on parameter assumptions. Evaluates to the value when the condition is known True and to Undefined when False.

parameters.name: cond
parameters.description: Condition under which expr is valid.

tools.example:
Integrate[x^a, {x, 0, 1}] (* ConditionalExpression[1/(1 + a), Re[a] > -1] *)
Assuming[a > 0, Integrate[x^a, {x, 0, 1}]] (* plain 1/(1+a) *)
Simplify[ConditionalExpression[Sqrt[x^2], x > 0]]
tools.notes: Use GenerateConditions -> False to suppress conditions, or Assuming/Refine to discharge them.

tools.name: Infinity
tools.description: The symbol for positive infinity, with -Infinity, ComplexInfinity and DirectedInfinity[z] for other infinite quantities. Arithmetic, Limit, Integrate, Sum, Plot ranges and Table/Range specifications all accept it; Infinity - Infinity yields Indeterminate.
tools.example:
Integrate[Exp[-x^2], {x, -Infinity, Infinity}]
Limit[1/x, x -> 0] (* ComplexInfinity *)
Min[{}] (* Infinity *)
tools.notes: Type Esc inf Esc in a notebook for the ∞ glyph. Infinity is exact; N[Infinity] stays Infinity. 1/0 gives ComplexInfinity with a Power::infy message.

tools.name: Indeterminate
tools.description: The symbol returned for undefined numerical results such as 0/0, 0*Infinity, Infinity - Infinity or Mean of a Cauchy distribution. It propagates through arithmetic and can be tested with SameQ or Cases to detect failed computations. Undefined is the analogue for symbolic functions evaluated outside their domain.
tools.example:
0/0 (* Indeterminate, with Power::indet *)
Mean[CauchyDistribution[0, 1]] (* Indeterminate *)
If[result === Indeterminate, Print["undefined"]]

tools.name: Null
tools.description: The symbol returned by expressions that produce no result, such as an empty CompoundExpression, Print, Do or a Set with a trailing semicolon; it is not displayed as output. Distinguish from Nothing (removed from lists) and Missing[] (absent data).
tools.example:
r = Do[i, {i, 3}]; r === Null (* True *)
DeleteCases[results, Null]

tools.name: BooleanMinimize
tools.description: Finds a minimal-size Boolean expression equivalent to expr in DNF (default), CNF, ANF or other forms, with an optional constraint expression for don't-care conditions. Use it to simplify logic circuits and conditions.
tools.usage:
BooleanMinimize[expr]
BooleanMinimize[expr, form]
BooleanMinimize[expr, form, cond]

parameters.name: cond
parameters.description: Don't-care condition: minimization need only agree where cond is True.

tools.example:
BooleanMinimize[(a && b) || (a && !b) || (!a && b)] (* a || b *)
BooleanMinimize[Xor[a, b, c], "CNF"]

tools.name: BooleanConvert
tools.description: Converts a Boolean expression to a canonical or structural form: "DNF", "CNF", "ANF", "NAND", "NOR", "ITE", "BFF" (binary decision diagram-like), and more. It does not minimize; combine with BooleanMinimize for compact results.
tools.example:
BooleanConvert[Implies[a, b] && Xor[b, c], "CNF"]
BooleanConvert[a || b, "NAND"]

tools.name: BooleanTable
tools.description: Gives the truth table of a Boolean expression over all assignments of its variables (as a list of True/False, or as rows with the inputs). Use it for verification, documentation and as training data for BooleanFunction.
tools.usage:
BooleanTable[expr]
BooleanTable[expr, {a, b, ...}]
BooleanTable[{expr1, expr2, ...}, {a, b, ...}]

parameters.name: {a, b, ...}
parameters.description: Variables in the order the table should iterate over.

tools.example:
BooleanTable[Implies[a, b], {a, b}] (* {True, False, True, True} *)
Grid[BooleanTable[{a, b, Xor[a, b]}, {a, b}] /. {True -> 1, False -> 0}]

tools.name: BooleanFunction
tools.description: Represents an arbitrary Boolean function by index, truth table, or DNF specification, as a compact BDD-based object that can be applied to arguments or converted with BooleanConvert. BooleanCountingFunction and BooleanConsecutiveFunction build threshold and run-length functions such as k-out-of-n.
tools.usage:
BooleanFunction[k, n]
BooleanFunction[{{in1, out1}, ...}]
BooleanFunction[tt][a, b, ...]
BooleanCountingFunction[k, n]
BooleanCountingFunction[{kmin, kmax}, {a, b, ...}]

parameters.name: k, n
parameters.description: Index k of an n-variable function, or count threshold k of n inputs.

parameters.name: tt
parameters.description: Truth table as a list of True/False.

tools.notes: BooleanCountingFunction is the natural way to express k-out-of-n reliability structures for ReliabilityDistribution.

tools.name: BooleanVariables
tools.description: Gives the list of Boolean variables appearing in an expression (or the number of variables of a BooleanFunction). Use it before BooleanTable or SatisfiabilityInstances when the variable set must be determined programmatically.
tools.example: BooleanVariables[(a || b) && !c] (* {a, b, c} *)

tools.name: SatisfiableQ
tools.description: Tests whether a Boolean expression has a satisfying assignment (SAT); TautologyQ tests whether it is True for all assignments. Both use an industrial SAT solver and handle thousands of variables.
tools.example:
SatisfiableQ[(a || b) && (!a || c) && !c && !b] (* False *)
TautologyQ[Or[a, !a]] (* True *)

tools.name: SatisfiabilityInstances
tools.description: Finds explicit assignments of the Boolean variables that make expr True (n instances, or All), returned as lists of True/False in variable order. SatisfiabilityCount gives the number of satisfying assignments (#SAT). Use them for constraint puzzles, scheduling and verification.
tools.usage:
SatisfiabilityInstances[expr, {a, b, ...}]
SatisfiabilityInstances[expr, {a, b, ...}, n]
SatisfiabilityInstances[expr, vars, All]
SatisfiabilityCount[expr]
tools.example:
SatisfiabilityInstances[Xor[a, b] && (a || c), {a, b, c}, 2]
SatisfiabilityCount[BooleanCountingFunction[{2, 2}, {a, b, c, d}]] (* 6 *)

tools.name: LogicalExpand
tools.description: Expands a logical expression into a disjunction of conjunctions (a non-minimized DNF), also distributing Not over And/Or and handling Equal/inequality conditions returned by Reduce. Use it to flatten nested conditions before further processing.

parameters.name: expr
parameters.description: Logical expression, possibly containing equations and inequalities.

tools.example:
LogicalExpand[(a || b) && (c || d)]
LogicalExpand[Reduce[x^2 == 1 && y > x, {x, y}]]

tools.name: Majority
tools.description: Gives True if more than half of its Boolean arguments are True (ties for an even count give False). A building block for voting logic, error-correcting decoders and cellular automaton rules.
tools.example:
Majority[True, False, True] (* True *)
BooleanMinimize[Majority[a, b, c]]

tools.name: Conjunction
tools.description: Conjunction[expr, {a, b, ...}] gives the And of expr over all Boolean values of the listed variables, and Disjunction the Or - the Boolean analogues of ForAll and Exists (quantifier elimination for Boolean variables).
tools.example:
Disjunction[a && b, {b}] (* a *)
Conjunction[Implies[a, b], {a}] (* b *)

tools.name: BitLength
tools.description: Gives the number of binary digits of an integer (BitLength[n] = Floor[Log2[n]] + 1 for n > 0); BitSet, BitClear and BitGet manipulate or read individual bits, complementing BitAnd/BitOr/BitXor/BitShiftLeft. Use them for bit-mask and flag arithmetic.
tools.usage:
BitLength[n]
BitSet[n, k]
BitClear[n, k]
BitGet[n, k]
BitNot[n]
BitShiftRight[n, k]
tools.example:
BitLength[255] (* 8 *)
BitSet[0, 3] (* 8 *)
BitGet[5, 0] (* 1 *)
BitShiftRight[1024, 3] (* 128 *)

tools.name: Order
tools.description: Gives 1, 0 or -1 according to whether e1 comes before, equals or comes after e2 in canonical order (the order used by Sort). OrderedQ tests whether a list is already in canonical (or custom) order. Use them for custom comparison functions and stability checks.
tools.example:
Order[a, b] (* 1 *)
OrderedQ[{1, 2, 2, 5}] (* True *)
Sort[exprs, Order[#1, #2] >= 0 &] (* reverse canonical order *)

tools.name: ListQ
tools.description: Structural head predicates: ListQ (head List), StringQ, AtomQ (no subparts), AssociationQ, BooleanQ (True or False) and ByteArrayQ. Use them for argument validation in function definitions and as pattern tests; for symbols use MatchQ[x, _Symbol] since there is no SymbolQ.
tools.example:
f[x_?ListQ] := Total[x]
AtomQ[3/4] (* True: rationals are atoms *)
BooleanQ[1] (* False *)
tools.notes: Head[expr] and MatchQ[expr, _List] are the general alternatives; for symbols use MatchQ[x, _Symbol].

tools.name: ValueQ
tools.description: Tests whether a symbol (or expression) has a value assigned, i.e. whether evaluating it would change it. Use it to initialise variables only once and to check for defined options; Method -> "OwnValues" and related settings restrict the kind of definition checked.
tools.example:
If[!ValueQ[cache], cache = <||>]
ValueQ[Pi] (* False: Pi has no OwnValue, though numeric *)
tools.notes: ValueQ has attribute HoldAll. Prefer Once or memoization patterns for expensive one-time initialisation.

tools.name: Exists
tools.description: Existential quantifier Exists[x, cond, expr] (with ForAll as the universal quantifier). Resolve and Reduce eliminate quantifiers over reals, complexes, integers or Booleans, giving conditions on the free variables - the basis for proving inequalities and checking feasibility.
tools.usage:
Exists[x, expr]
Exists[{x, y}, cond, expr]
Resolve[Exists[x, x^2 + b x + c == 0], Reals]
tools.example:
Resolve[Exists[x, x^2 + b x + c == 0], Reals] (* b^2 - 4 c >= 0 *)
Resolve[ForAll[x, x^2 - 2 a x + 1 > 0], Reals]

tools.name: UnateQ
tools.description: Tests whether a Boolean expression is unate (monotone in each variable: positive or negative unate) in all or specified variables. Used in logic synthesis and in checking monotonicity of reliability structure functions.
tools.example:
UnateQ[a && (b || c)] (* True *)
UnateQ[Xor[a, b]] (* False *)

tools.name: ShiftRegisterSequence
tools.description: Generates a linear-feedback shift register (LFSR) sequence for a given tap specification and length, producing maximal-length pseudo-random binary sequences used in communications, CRC and test-pattern generation.
tools.usage:
ShiftRegisterSequence[n]
ShiftRegisterSequence[{taps, n}, len]
ShiftRegisterSequence[{taps, n}, {init}, len]
tools.example: ShiftRegisterSequence[{{3, 4}, 4}, 15] (* maximal-length 4-bit LFSR *)
